The **source pinning** is **high** (documented restriction, universal in surveyed rulesets). The **exact long-run `needs:` membership** is only as good as the guard, which is **high** locally and unproven on a runner until P03. The **pollers-rejected** and **org-workflows-rejected** calls are **medium**: design-grounded, but the poller sources were not re-fetched here. **What neither leg nor this synthesis supplies**: no hosted-runner behavior was measured by anyone, and criteria 5–8 are proposals.

consumed.ci-job-structure: one .github/workflows/ci.yml whose jobs are partitioned by whether a check compiles Rust, never by which check it is. Tier 0 is a single always-run detector job named plan on ubuntu-latest carrying no toolchain, no cache action and no target/ directory: after actions/checkout with fetch-depth 0 and persist-credentials false it runs one bash step under set -euo pipefail that computes git diff --no-ext-diff --no-textconv --no-renames --name-only from BASE_SHA to HEAD, so the path list includes the source side of every rename, with BASE_SHA read from github.event.pull_request.base.sha through the step env block, treats every file name as data and never evaluates it, and writes exactly four job outputs - code, web, workflows, docs - as the literal strings true or false and never as any other value, publishing true on all four for every event whose name is not pull_request so that pushes to main and merge-queue entries are never skip-gated. Every output that gates a required check fails closed, whether the check compiles or not, so a path nobody anticipated runs the gate rather than skipping it, and the body makes that structural - code and web start true and are set false only on affirmative proof that every changed path is skippable, a grep exit of 1, never on a match, an error or a test cut short, and workflows and docs likewise start true and are set false only on a grep exit of 1, and every path test reads the whole list from a here-string rather than through a pipeline whose early-exiting grep can end it under pipefail: code is the negation of a skip-list of paths that cannot affect a compile, a package or an installed artifact, with every entry of the package include allow-list R49 owns forced non-skippable because each of them is a packaging input, and with no skip-list entry allowed to match a file any package contains - so the Markdown entry matches only root-level files. Markdown under docs/ and .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/ stays skippable through those directory entries, and no entry matches anything under src/ or a member directory, because src/ is packaged and a workspace member that names no include list packages its whole directory; web is fail-closed too - every change that sets code also sets web, because the web member depends on the core member and the root package that hosts the serve binary depends on every member, and web is additionally set by any change under the web member's directory, so the paths R69 names are a subset of the rule rather than its whole; workflows gates only workflow-lint and its pattern contains the whole input of every check in that job by construction - the workflow files, the local actions they call, which live under .github/actions/, and the workflow linter's own config file; docs keys on the prose tree and gates no job in this file, because R82's link check is a step of hygiene, so it is kept only as a literal output that no check whose input another item declares may consume; and a fifth key is added only when some job would be skipped by it that code does not already skip, and is itself written as the negation of a skip-list, or, if it gates only a job that compiles nothing, as a pattern containing that job's whole input. Tier 1 is the checks that compile nothing, each its own cheap job carrying no cache step: hygiene, which deliberately has no needs edge so that a formatter failure still reports on a pull request whose compile tier is skipped, and which hosts every non-compiling check whose input no key contains, R29's non-code formatting slot and R20's two action-pin checks included, as is R82's link check, while R82's rustdoc part is the doc build step of check; and workflow-lint, gated on workflows, which hosts only checks whose whole input is the workflow tree. Tier 2 is the checks that compile: ONE job named check per entry of target-os-matrix through a strategy matrix over os alone with fail-fast false - never a matrix dimension over Cargo features, because the cache action keys on the job id and not on matrix values - running clippy with the feature off, clippy with the feature on, a no-default-features check of the facade, cargo test with the feature off scoped by -p to the non-web packages so the feature-off property is proven rather than assumed, cargo test over the workspace with the feature on, a build of the serve binary and a doc build, as ordered steps sharing one target/, every cargo command carrying --locked, where each cargo step runs under !cancelled() so that one failing step does not hide the results of the steps after it; plus msrv-floor, a separate single-runner job rather than a matrix leg of check because the floor needs only the declared-floor check Cargo's own CI guide shows rather than check's whole step list, verifying the declared rust-version on ubuntu-latest, which widens to every runner by substituting the matrix os expression into runs-on if the owner answers the open F033 cross-product question that way; plus install-smoke, R50's one ubuntu-latest job, whose web leg is a step conditioned on the web output. Every gated job consumes the detector through needs: plan and a POSITIVE predicate of the form needs.plan.outputs.KEY == 'true', never a negated one, and carrying no status function, so that the platform's implicit success() skips every gated job whenever plan fails or is skipped, under either polarity; the positive form is kept for consistency with R18, R86 and the dorny/paths-filter example, because the one remaining empty-key case, a misspelled output name, is caught by lint on the consumer side and by the detector cases on the producer side, and because a consumer that opts out of skip propagation with always() or !cancelled() must read plan's result, never plan's outputs, as its condition; actionlint type-checks the output name and the needs edge but does NOT reject the negated form, so that rule travels in prose to every consumer rather than being left to lint. A failed plan skips every gated job and skipped is a successful check status, so a failed plan must itself fail a required check; this file hands that constraint on without deciding how it is met: either plan is itself a required check, or an aggregate, if R12 chooses one, includes plan in its needs and treats a failure or cancelled result of plan as failure. ci.yml carries no trigger-level paths or paths-ignore filter of any kind, because a workflow skipped by path filtering leaves its checks Pending and blocks merging while a job skipped by a conditional reports Success; its triggers are pull_request and push restricted to main, plus merge_group so a queue's speculative merge still reports; it declares an empty workflow-level permissions map with a per-job re-grant whose scopes are R08's; and it declares workflow-level concurrency with cancel-in-progress true on a group keyed to the workflow plus the pull-request number, falling back to the commit sha when there is no pull request, so a force-push cancels the superseded pull-request run while consecutive pushes to main never cancel one another and keep populating the cache. This file holds no aggregate required-status job, which is R12's, and no release, secret-scanning, devcontainer or AI-review job, which are separate workflow files. Every further check arrives as a named slot under one rule: a check that compiles nothing is a step of hygiene, or its own cheap job behind a path gate only when that gate's key contains the whole input of every check in the job; a check that compiles what check already compiles is an ordered step of check; and a check needing its own toolchain, its own runner or a target/ it must not share becomes its own job with needs: plan and a positive predicate, counted against a ceiling of roughly six cache-bearing job ids per runner, where the budget arithmetic is the sum over cache-bearing job ids of that job id's runner count. Any single-job workflow file that compiles no Rust, R17's scanner included, lands on ubuntu-latest, because it neither shares nor claims a target/ cache entry and gains nothing from a second runner

fixed.msrv-policy: stable minus 2 minor versions, raised only in a minor release, declared as rust-version in Cargo.toml and tested in CI

principles:
**The shared requirement, its source, and the level at which agreement is required.** No change merges unless every quality gate that applied to it passed; a gate that legitimately did not apply must not block it; a gate that failed, was cancelled, or never produced a verdict must block it; and only the CI app's verdict counts. Source: py's header comment ("`ci-ok` is the single required status for branch protection (skipped jobs count as ok)", `S-py-header`), the vendor's required-checks pages (`S-docs-*`), and R11's handover ("a failed `plan` must itself fail a required check", R11 `DECISION.md:180`).

| ID | Principle | Agreement level across py / ts / rs |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | **Gate completeness.** Every blocking check blocks the merge when it fails, is cancelled, or never ran for an unexplained reason | **policy** — must agree in all three |
| P2 | **The blocking set lives in version control.** The out-of-band settings reduce to a minimal, stable set of names defined by a reviewed file | **policy** — must agree; the file format may vary |
| P3 | **A skip passes only when a trusted decision caused it.** `skipped` is a pass only because R11's detector fails closed *and* the detector's own failure is folded into the verdict | **policy** — must agree wherever skip-gating exists |
| P4 | **Source authenticity.** Only the CI app can satisfy the required context | **policy** — must agree |
| P5 | **Merge-queue parity.** The same context reports on the queue's speculative merge | **capability** — must agree wherever a merge queue is used; vacuous in a repository that uses none (ts today, `T-ts-noqueue`). rs adopts the trigger through F025 |

**What must agree and what may vary.** P1–P5 must agree across the three repositories, P5 wherever a merge queue is used: the threat and the platform are identical, and nothing about Python, TypeScript or Rust changes how GitHub evaluates a required check. The mechanism may vary — a `jq` line, a shell loop, or an action — and the context name *should* agree (`ci-ok`) for a concrete reason: one shared name lets one organization ruleset gate every blueprint repository. That last point is a convenience proposal, not a correctness requirement.

**Essential behaviors, with observable acceptance criteria.**

| # | Behavior | Observable acceptance criterion |
|---|---|---|
| B1 | One stable check name gates the merge | Settings require exactly one CI check name; adding or renaming a job never needs a settings change |
| B2 | A legitimately skipped gate does not block | A docs-only pull request shows the aggregate green while gated jobs report skipped |
| B3 | Any failed gate blocks | One failing job turns the aggregate red and the pull request unmergeable |
| B4 | A cancelled run blocks rather than passing silently | A cancelled run leaves the aggregate non-green |
| B5 | A failed detector blocks | A forced `plan` failure leaves the pull request unmergeable (R11 criterion 13) |
| B6 | Merge-queue entries report | A `merge_group` run produces a green aggregate on success, never a stuck "Expected" |

**The architectural alternatives, compared before any tool.**

| Architecture | What settings name | Who defines the blocking set | Failed-`plan` hazard | Crosses files | Template portability | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A. Hand-rolled aggregate, allow-list, guard, pinned (recommended) | 1 per gating workflow | the reviewed `ci.yml` | structural: `plan` in `needs:` | no | good: one stable name | **Selected** |
| B. Naive aggregate (`needs` only, unconditional step) | 1 | the reviewed file | fails open: the aggregate skips and the skip reads as success | no | good but wrong | **Excluded** (Disagreement 5) |
| C. Aggregate via `re-actors/alls-green` | 1 | the file plus action inputs | yes, with `allowed-skips` maintained | no | good | **Ranked runner-up** |
| D. Per-job required checks, no aggregate | 7 today, changing with the matrix and every rename | repository admin, out of band | only if `plan` is also listed — an easy omission | yes, by listing | poor: PROBLEM-15 | **Second runner-up** |
| E. Single job, nothing to aggregate | 1 (the job) | the file trivially | n/a | n/a | good | **Unavailable**: R11 settled six job ids with skip-gating |
| F. Check-run poller across workflows | 1 | whatever ran on the commit | only via API reads | **yes** | good, at a token + polling cost | **Rejected** on design (Disagreement 9) |
| G. Organization "Require workflows to pass" | a workflow, not a job | organization settings | yes | yes | organization-owned repos only | **Rejected**: a template cannot assume its adopter's ownership |

**Why the allow-list, not py's deny-list (Disagreement 1, adjudicated).** Four decision rules were executed against nine needs-vectors (`r12-verdict.sh`; the recommended rule and py's loop were both extracted from their files, not retyped):

| Case | Recommended allow-list | py deny-list (real bytes) | cargo all-`success` | naive `!contains(failure)` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T1 all success | PASS | PASS | PASS | PASS |
| T2 docs-only, gated jobs skipped | PASS | PASS | **FAIL** | PASS |
| T3 `plan` failed, gated skipped | FAIL | FAIL | FAIL | FAIL |
| T4 `plan` cancelled, gated skipped | FAIL | FAIL | FAIL | **PASS** |
| T5 one `check` leg failed | FAIL | FAIL | FAIL | FAIL |
| T6 `check` cancelled | FAIL | FAIL | FAIL | **PASS** |
| T7 `hygiene` failed | FAIL | FAIL | FAIL | FAIL |
| T8 unrecognized result value | FAIL | **PASS** | FAIL | **PASS** |
| T9 empty `needs` | FAIL | **PASS** | **PASS** | **PASS** |

The deny-list passes anything it does not name (T8) and passes vacuously when there is nothing to inspect (T9; `all()` over `{}` is `true`, `V0-empty`). R11's fail-closed policy — every required gate, compiling or not — requires the allow-list spelling plus the `length > 0` guard. The cost is one `jq` line instead of a shell loop; `jq` 1.7 ships on the runner (`S-runner-jq`), and the `jq`-over-`toJSON(needs)` form is what the rust-lang and Astral aggregates use. The py follow-on proposes the same spelling there.

**Why `always()`, and why `!cancelled()` is accepted (Disagreement 3, adjudicated).** Without either, a failed dependency skips the aggregate (`S-docs-skipprop`), and a skipped job reports Success (`S-docs-skipped-success`) — a false green; `actionlint` accepts that broken shape (`L2`), so the `if:` line travels in prose and review. Between the two forms: the vendor's required-check page prescribes `always()` (`S-docs-always`), R11's slot row prescribes it, and py uses it. The feared hazard of `!cancelled()` — a cancelled run leaving the aggregate `skipped`-green — did not materialize in 9 of 9 sampled cancelled runs: 6 of 6 `!cancelled()` aggregates (cargo, rust-analyzer) concluded `cancelled`, and 3 of 3 `always()` aggregates (uv) ran and concluded `success` (`S-cancelled-*`). The uv sample shows only that an `always()` aggregate *runs* in a cancelled run: in all three, the cancelled jobs (`bench`, `build-docker` and `build-release-artifacts` in all three, `review` in two, `test-smoke` in one) are outside the `needs:` of uv's aggregate `required-checks-passed`, so no sample exercises a cancelled `needs:` member turning the aggregate red. That case rests on the local T4/T6 rows and on criterion 6 for P03. The docs' hang warning against `always()` does not apply: `ci-ok` has no checkout, no network, and a 5-minute cap. `!cancelled()` remains an accepted equivalent; the sample is small and contains no hand-cancelled head run of an open pull request (P03 checks it).

**Why the guard is part of the pattern, not advice (Disagreement 2, adjudicated).** A job left out of `needs:` is invisible to *every* verdict rule, and lint does not catch it either (`L3`). That is not hypothetical: rust-analyzer's `conclusion` omits its `changes` detector while `typescript` is gated on that detector's outputs (`S-ra-drift`) — so a failed detector skips `typescript` and the aggregate counts the skip as a pass, exactly the hazard R11 hands over. py kept its in-repo list in sync across 21 revisions by review alone (`S-py-history`), which proves review *can* work, not that it always does. The guard closes the mode mechanically: it exits 0 on the fixture and exits 1 naming the jobs when one is added (`G2`), when `plan` is dropped (`G3`), and when one is renamed (`G4`). It costs one `yq | jq` step in a job that already checks out the tree (`yq` 4.53.6 on the runner, `S-runner-yq`).

**Why no `merge_group` logic (the LOW question).** Nothing extra is needed in the aggregate. R11 already puts `merge_group` in `ci.yml`'s triggers and publishes `true` on every detector output for non-`pull_request` events, so nothing is skip-gated in the queue; `ci-ok` runs there like any job (P03 verifies live queue reporting under criterion 8). Two conditions must hold: the queue's required check is the same `ci-ok` context, and the name is unique across workflow files (`S-docs-unique`) — clippy's per-workflow aggregates show the shape. Without the trigger, the required check never reports and every queue entry deadlocks at "Expected" — py documents that failure mode in its own file header.

**Matrix legs need no special handling.** The platform folds `check`'s per-OS legs into one per-job result, so one `needs:` entry covers both runners. The same matrix is part of why the aggregate pays: without it, `check (ubuntu-latest)` and `check (macos-latest)` are two settings entries that change whenever the owner-fixed matrix changes — ts's matrixed `ci` job shows the one-job version of that cost with its two `continuous-integration` contexts.

**Does the value depend on R11 (the first HIGH question)? It depends on multi-context CI, not specifically on skip-gating — and R11 settled multi-context CI.** Without any skip-gating the aggregate still pays: the matrix contexts above, plus the template argument (settings do not copy into generated repositories; PROBLEM-15). With R11's skip-gating the aggregate is load-bearing rather than merely convenient: a failed `plan` skips every gated job, and a skipped job reports success. Under a single-job, non-matrix shape the aggregate would be pure overhead and E would win — that branch is decided fact in the other direction since R11 revision 7.

**Fitness gates, answered before popularity is weighed.** (1) License: `inapplicable` per the owner ruling above; `alls-green`'s `BSD-3-Clause` is a figure, not a gate result. (2) MSRV: `inapplicable` — a workflow file, a `jq` line and a composite Python action have no `rust-version`. (3) RustSec / `unsafe`: `inapplicable` — no crate enters any dependency tree; RustSec does not cover GitHub Actions. Security posture of the pick, stated directly: no checkout, `permissions: {}`, no secrets, no expression interpolated into shell (`L5-nointerp`). (4) OS matrix: passes in adapted form — the aggregate needs only a hosted runner with `bash` and `jq`, true of both matrix entries; it is pinned to `ubuntu-latest` (cheapest, no toolchain, no cache, matching `plan`). (5) Default features / async-runtime coupling: `inapplicable` — nothing is linked into the template. (6) Binary size / compile time: `inapplicable` to the artifact; CI cost is one ~10-second job per run plus one `yq | jq` step in `workflow-lint`. No candidate is excluded by a fitness gate; B is excluded by this item's own fail-closed requirement (Disagreement 5).

**Cross-ecosystem realization (the third HIGH question).** P1, P2 and P4 are required in all three repositories, P3 in each one that skip-gates, and P5 in each one that uses a merge queue; only the mechanism varies where structure forces it. rs realizes them with the aggregate above over R11's six job ids — same platform, same skip-gating design as py, same hardened form, same `ci-ok` name (a shared low-level value justified by identical tradeoffs: same vendor, same verdict semantics, one organization ruleset able to gate every blueprint). py already realizes them with `ci-ok`; its two weaknesses are the deny-list spelling (T8/T9) and the unguarded `needs:` — both fixed by the follow-on below, for which this answer supplies the rationale. ts lacks P1, P2 and P4 today: it has a required-capable job, `ci`, but requires no check at all (`S-ts-unprotected`, `S-ts-norule`), so no gate blocks a merge (P1), the blocking set is not defined anywhere (P2), and there is no required context to pin (P4). P3 is vacuous for ts, because the P3 row scopes it to repositories with skip-gating and ts has none. P5 is vacuous until ts adopts a merge queue: ts has no `merge_queue` rule, and without a queue there is no speculative merge to report on (`T-ts-noqueue`). This is missing capability per the BASELINE-REVIEW finding, not drift and not a justified difference. ts's advisory `bun-lane` is correctly non-voting and is not part of the gap (`T-ts-bunlane`). If ts ever promotes a second job to required, P1 requires the aggregate in form A, not B.

**py and ts follow-on (rationale only; no change made here).** py: switch the result test to the positive allow-list plus `length > 0`; add the guard; fold `lint.yml`'s five individually required jobs behind a `lint-ok` aggregate (its live protection requires 8 contexts, `S-py-live`). ts, in order of necessity:

1. **Require a check at all.** This is the only step P1 forces.
2. **Fold `ci`'s two matrix contexts behind one `ci-ok`**, so the required name does not move with the Node matrix. `ci-ok`'s `needs:` is `[ci]` only.
3. **Keep `bun-lane` out of `needs:`.** It is a non-voting job, so under the rule in `### Consumers` below it does not join the allow-list as-is. Keeping it out of `needs:` entirely is sufficient for ts, because nothing in ts's verdict has to observe it.
4. **If ts also adopts the guard**, the guard's "job set minus `ci-ok` equals `needs:`" test would fail on `bun-lane`, so ts's guard needs a stated exception. The rationale proposes deriving that exception from the file itself: the guard's voting set is the job set minus `ci-ok` minus every job whose `continue-on-error` is literally `true`. On ts's file that derivation yields exactly `{ci}`, with `bun-lane` the only advisory job (`T-ts-voting`). It needs no second maintained list. The alternative the non-voting rule reopens is alls-green with `allowed-failures: bun-lane`; the derived exception is preferred for ts because it keeps the one-line `jq` verdict and adds no third-party action. The derived exception is proposed, not executed as a guard here; `T-ts-voting` checks only the derivation over ts's file.
5. **Add `merge_group` when ts adopts a merge queue**, not before; F025 is an rs adoption and does not bind ts until then.

This follow-on is the controller's to route; it changes neither rs's guard nor the rs rule for a future non-voting job.

**Minimal realistic example.** `review/evidence/ci.candidate.yml` (101 lines): R11's six job ids as skeletons with placeholder steps, the recommended `ci-ok` job, and the guard step in `workflow-lint`. It lints clean (`L1`); both R12-owned `run:` bodies are `shellcheck`-clean when extracted (`L4`); every recommended byte is asserted literally (`L5-*`).
